name: whiteboard
description: Hand-drawn whiteboard stickman animation — bean-body characters, ink illustrations, and draw-in animations on warm parchment. Optimized for entertainment, comedy, storytelling, and educational content.

sceneTypeDescriptions.title-card: Opening title or episode title — large hand-lettered text, minimal illustration, sets the tone. Static camera.
sceneTypeDescriptions.establishing: Wide shot that sets the scene — shows location, time of day, and characters in context. Environment-heavy, character(s) small. Static camera.
sceneTypeDescriptions.action: Dynamic scene with movement — running, jumping, chasing, fighting, falling. Exaggerated poses, motion lines, speed streaks. Camera pans to follow action.
sceneTypeDescriptions.dialogue: Two or more characters talking — speech bubbles, expressive faces, gestures. Focus on upper bodies and faces. Camera may zoom to speaker.
sceneTypeDescriptions.reaction: Close-up on a character's emotional response — the comedy/drama beat. Oversized head, exaggerated expression, minimal background. Camera zooms to face.
sceneTypeDescriptions.montage: Multiple mini-scenes in one frame — time passing, a sequence of events, before/after. Laid out as 2-4 vignettes with divider lines or time arrows.
sceneTypeDescriptions.closeup: Tight framing on a specific object, prop, or detail — a phone screen, a letter, a clock showing the time. Starts zoomed, minimal movement.
sceneTypeDescriptions.transition: Bridge between scenes — a visual gag, a wipe, a character walking off-screen. Camera move IS the transition (zoom out, pan away, fade).
sceneTypeDescriptions.teaching: Educational/explainer moment — character at a whiteboard, diagram, or pointing to a concept. Draw-in animation reveals the concept as narrator explains.
sceneTypeDescriptions.list: Numbered or bulleted points appearing one by one — each item draws in sequentially. Static camera, item reveals provide motion.
sceneTypeDescriptions.closing: Final scene — summary, call to action, or emotional landing. May echo the opening. Optional slow pull-back camera.

punctuationEffects.emDash: dramatic pause for reveal or punchline

intakeQuestions.question: What is the video about? Describe the story, scenario, or concept. (e.g., 'A programmer's typical Monday morning', 'Two friends argue about pineapple on pizza', 'How to survive a boring meeting')
Who are the characters? List names and brief descriptions (e.g., 'Dave — tired office worker, always has coffee; Karen — overly enthusiastic manager'). Or type 'auto' to let the script writer decide:
What is the tone?
options: storytelling — narrative arc, emotional beats, character-driven
educational — teach a concept with humor and visual metaphors
satire — social commentary with wit and irony

intakeQuestions.question: List 3-6 key scenes or beats (comma-separated, or 'auto' to let the script writer decide):
How long should the video be?

scriptStyle.narrator: witty conversational storyteller, confident and expressive, like a friend acting out a story
scriptStyle.register: casual, slightly irreverent, personality-driven warmth with comedic timing
patterns: comedic beats with pauses for visual punchlines ('And then... yep. That happened.')
character voice shifts for dialogue (slightly different cadence per character)
setup-punchline rhythm (describe the situation, then land the joke with the illustration)
rhetorical questions that set up visual gags ('You know what happens next, right?')
callbacks to earlier scenes ('Remember that coffee? Yeah, it's cold now.')
short declarative sentences for emphasis and timing
antiPatterns: long complex sentences that kill comedic timing
explaining the joke (let the illustration land it)
monotone energy — every scene needs distinct vocal energy
narrating exactly what the viewer can already see
